name: Catalyst Climbing Harness
title: Catalyst Climbing Harness for Tree Work
meta: The Catalyst climbing harness is a European-style arborist saddle with a bridge attachment for rope work. See how it fits, what to check, and typical price.
tagline: A European-style bridge saddle for climbers who spend long days on rope.
summary: The Catalyst climbing harness is a European-style arborist saddle built around a bridge attachment, so your hitch or device can travel side to side as you work the canopy. It suits climbers who want a modern bridge saddle for both MRS and SRS.
highlights: European-style bridge saddle for tree work
Bridge lets the tie-in point slide as you move
Works with MRS hitch systems and SRS devices
Gear loops for carabiners, saws, and accessories
Adjustable waist and leg loops for fit

body.h: How a bridge saddle works in the tree
p: On a bridge saddle your climbing system clips to a short length of rope or webbing between the leg loops rather than to fixed D-rings. That lets the attachment point roll with you as you face a new limb, which keeps the hitch in front of you and cuts down on twisting at the hips.
For long limb walks and pruning days, that freedom of movement is what most climbers notice first. Pair the bridge with a ring or swivel if you run an SRS device and want to keep it oriented.

Bridge saddles also spread load across the waist and legs differently from a fixed-D saddle. Spend a few climbs adjusting the bridge length: shorter keeps your device close and easy to tend, longer gives more swing room. Write down the setting that works so you can repeat it after you replace the bridge.

Try the saddle on and hang in it low before you climb. The waist belt should sit above the hips and the leg loops should take the weight without pinching. Check the bridge every day for glazing, cuts, and wear at the connectors, and replace it on the manufacturer's schedule or sooner if it looks tired.

Compare it with other European saddles before you buy, since fit varies a lot between makers. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Is the Catalyst climbing harness good for SRS?
faq.a: A bridge saddle like this is commonly used for both SRS and MRS. Follow the manufacturer's instructions for approved attachment points and connectors for your device.

faq.q: How often should the bridge be replaced?
faq.a: Inspect it before every climb and replace it when you see glazing, cuts, or fuzzing, or on the manufacturer's recommended schedule, whichever comes first.

name: DMM Kinisi Pro Arborist Harness
title: DMM Kinisi Pro Arborist Harness: Fit and Features
meta: The DMM Kinisi Pro is a lightweight bridge saddle for working arborists. Learn how it climbs on MRS and SRS, what to inspect, and its typical street price.
tagline: DMM's pro-level bridge saddle for climbers who want light weight and free movement.
summary: The DMM Kinisi Pro is DMM's top arborist harness, a bridge saddle designed to stay light and move with you on long climbs. It is aimed at full-time climbers working both MRS and SRS systems.
highlights: Pro-level arborist bridge saddle from DMM
Light build for long days in the canopy
Bridge attachment for free side-to-side movement
Gear loops and accessory points for saws and hardware
Made for MRS and SRS climbing

body.h: Why climbers choose the Kinisi Pro
p: DMM has a long history in climbing hardware, and the Kinisi Pro brings that thinking to the saddle. The goal is a harness that disappears when you are working: a bridge that lets your system follow you around the stem, leg loops that carry the load without hot spots, and a layout that keeps your gear where your hands expect it.
It is a good match for climbers who spend most of the day on rope doing removals, pruning, or storm work and want less bulk at the hips.

A lighter saddle pays off late in the day. Less weight on the hips means less fatigue on repeated ascents, and a clean layout means fewer snagged lanyards and slings when you are moving through tight canopy. Think about how you rack your gear before you buy, so the loops and attachment points match the way you actually work.

body.h: Setting it up and keeping it in service
p: Adjust the waist and legs on the ground, then hang test low with your full kit attached. Check stitching, buckles, the bridge, and every connector before each climb. Retire the saddle if you find cuts, heat damage, or chemical contact, and keep it away from bar oil and fuel in the truck.

See our other European saddles if you want to compare fit. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: What is the difference between the Kinisi and Kinisi Pro?
faq.a: The Pro is DMM's higher-spec version aimed at full-time climbers. Check DMM's current product information for the exact differences in padding and features.

faq.q: Can I use the Kinisi Pro with a mechanical SRS device?
faq.a: Yes, bridge saddles are widely used with SRS devices. Use only the attachment points and connectors the manufacturer approves.

name: Fox Harness by R-Easy Climbing (Fabric)
title: Fox Harness by R-Easy Climbing, Fabric Version
meta: The fabric Fox harness by R-Easy Climbing is a European-style tree climbing saddle. See who it suits, how to fit it, and what to inspect before each climb.
tagline: A fabric European-style tree climbing saddle for working arborists.
summary: The Fox harness by R-Easy Climbing, fabric version, is a European-style tree climbing saddle for arborists who want a breathable textile build. It was offered on pre-order, so check current availability before planning around it.
highlights: European-style arborist saddle
Fabric version for a lighter, more breathable feel
Designed for rope-based tree climbing
Gear loops for hardware and tools
Also offered in a leather version

p: The Fox comes in fabric and leather versions. Fabric saddles tend to be lighter and dry faster after a wet morning, which many climbers prefer in summer heat. Leather has a classic feel and wears in over time but needs more care to keep it supple.
Either way, the job is the same: hold you comfortably in work position while you rig, prune, or take down wood, and keep your tools organized on the hips.

European-style saddles usually put the attachment on a bridge or sliding ring, so you can rotate around the stem without your system pulling you sideways. That suits climbers who spend long stretches working out on limbs. Before buying any pre-order saddle, check sizing information carefully, because returns and exchanges can take longer than with stocked items.

Size the saddle with the clothing you climb in, then hang test with your full rack. Check stitching, buckles, and the attachment points before every climb, and keep the saddle away from fuel, bar oil, and sharp tools in the truck.

Browse our European saddles to compare options. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Is the Fox harness still available?
faq.a: It was listed as a pre-order item. Availability can change, so use the price check button to see current stock.

faq.q: Should I choose fabric or leather?
faq.a: Fabric is usually lighter and dries faster. Leather wears in over time but needs regular conditioning. Pick the one that suits your climate and care habits.

name: Fox Harness by R-Easy Climbing (Leather)
title: Fox Harness by R-Easy Climbing, Leather Version
meta: The leather Fox harness by R-Easy Climbing is a European-style arborist saddle with a classic leather build. Learn how to fit it and care for the leather.
tagline: The leather version of the Fox European-style tree climbing saddle.
summary: The Fox harness leather version from R-Easy Climbing is a European-style arborist saddle for climbers who like the feel and durability of leather. It was sold on pre-order, so confirm current availability before you count on it.
highlights: European-style arborist saddle
Leather build for a classic feel
Designed for rope-based tree climbing
Gear loops for hardware and tools
Also offered in a fabric version

body.h: Why some climbers still want leather
p: Leather saddles have a long history in tree work. A good one breaks in to your shape and stands up to bark, sawdust, and daily handling. The trade-off is weight and care: leather takes longer to dry and needs conditioning so it does not crack.
If you climb in cooler weather or simply prefer the feel, the leather Fox is the version to look at. In hot, wet conditions the fabric version may be the better pick.

Because the leather version will break in over the first few weeks, expect some stiffness at first. Wear it on a few easy climbs before relying on it for a long day, and readjust the waist and leg straps once the leather has settled. Keep the fabric version in mind if you climb mostly in heat or rain.

Let it dry slowly at room temperature, never next to a heater. Clean off sap and grime, condition the leather with a product the manufacturer approves, and inspect stitching, buckles, and attachment points before every climb.

Compare it with other European saddles. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: How do I dry a wet leather saddle?
faq.a: Hang it at room temperature away from direct heat. Fast drying can stiffen and crack leather.

faq.q: Is the leather version heavier than the fabric one?
faq.a: Leather saddles are generally heavier than textile saddles. Check the manufacturer's listing for exact weights.

name: Teufelberger treeMOTION Essential Climbing Saddle
title: Teufelberger treeMOTION Essential Climbing Saddle
meta: The Teufelberger treeMOTION Essential is a streamlined bridge saddle in the treeMOTION family. See who it suits, how to fit it, and the typical street price.
tagline: A pared-back treeMOTION bridge saddle for climbers who want the core design.
summary: The treeMOTION Essential is Teufelberger's streamlined take on its well-known treeMOTION bridge saddle, keeping the core design without every extra. It suits climbers moving up to a bridge saddle and pros who want a simpler setup.
highlights: Part of Teufelberger's treeMOTION saddle family
Bridge attachment for free movement
Streamlined design with the core features
Works for MRS and SRS climbing
Gear loops for hardware and tools

p: The treeMOTION name is one of the most common sights in tree crews, and the Essential carries over the feature that made it popular: a bridge that lets your climbing system move with you instead of pulling you off line. The aim is a saddle that is easy to set up and easy to live with.
It is a sensible choice for a climber's first bridge saddle, or for crews outfitting several climbers who want a consistent, simple harness.

A bridge saddle changes how your hitch or device sits compared with a fixed D-ring saddle, so plan a few practice climbs on easy trees. Get used to how the bridge lets you turn, how your lanyard rides, and where your saw and hand tools hang before you take it onto a demanding removal.

Adjust the waist and leg loops on the ground and hang test with your kit before climbing. Inspect the bridge, stitching, and buckles before every climb, and replace the bridge on Teufelberger's schedule or when it shows wear.

See our full range of European saddles. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: How is the treeMOTION Essential different from other treeMOTION saddles?
faq.a: It is a more streamlined model in the same family. Check Teufelberger's current listing for the exact feature differences.

faq.q: Is it a good first bridge saddle?
faq.a: It is a sensible option for climbers moving to a bridge saddle. Get trained on the setup and hang test before climbing.

name: 8mm Black Beeline Eye-to-Eye Prusik
title: 8mm Black Beeline Eye-to-Eye Prusik Hitch Cord
meta: The 8mm black Beeline eye-to-eye prusik is a hitch cord with an eye at each end for friction hitches. See how it is used and what to check before you climb.
tagline: An 8 mm black eye-to-eye hitch cord for friction hitches on climbing lines.
summary: The 8mm black Beeline eye-to-eye prusik is a hitch cord with an eye at each end, ready to tie a Distel, VT, or similar friction hitch on your climbing line. It is a common piece of everyday MRS and SRS kit.
highlights: 8 mm hitch cord
Eye at each end for clipping to a carabiner
For Distel, VT, and other friction hitches
Black color is easy to tell apart on the saddle

p: An eye-to-eye prusik ties around your climbing line and clips back to a carabiner, so it grips under load and slides when you tend it. Most climbers pair it with a micro pulley above the hitch so slack can be taken up with one hand.
Hitch behavior depends on the pairing of cord and rope. An 8 mm cord is a common match for 11 to 13 mm climbing lines, but test it low on your own rope before you trust it at height.

Hitch cord color is more useful than it sounds. When you carry two or three cords on the saddle, a distinct color tells you at a glance which one is which, so you grab the right length and blend for the rope you are on. It also makes it easier to track how old each cord is.

Hitch cords take a lot of heat and abrasion. Check for glazing, stiff or flattened sections, and worn eyes before every climb, and replace the cord at the first sign of damage. Keep a spare in the gear bag.

Find other eye-and-eye prusiks in different lengths and blends. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: What rope diameter does an 8 mm hitch cord suit?
faq.a: It is commonly used on 11 to 13 mm climbing lines. Always test the hitch low on your actual rope.

faq.q: How long does a hitch cord last?
faq.a: It depends on use and heat. Inspect it every climb and retire it when you see glazing, stiffness, or worn eyes.

name: Courant Phoenix Pink Dragon 8mm Sewn Eye-to-Eye Prusik
title: Courant Phoenix 8mm Sewn Eye-to-Eye Prusik
h1: Courant Phoenix Pink Dragon 8mm Sewn Eye-to-Eye Prusik
meta: The Courant Phoenix eye to eye prusik is an 8 mm sewn hitch cord in Pink Dragon color for friction hitches. See how it pairs with ropes and when to retire it.
tagline: An 8 mm sewn eye-to-eye hitch cord from Courant in Pink Dragon color.
summary: The Courant Phoenix eye to eye prusik is an 8 mm hitch cord with sewn eyes, made for tying friction hitches on your climbing line. The Pink Dragon color makes it easy to spot on a busy saddle.
highlights: 8 mm Courant Phoenix hitch cord
Sewn eyes at both ends
For Distel, VT, and other friction hitches
Pink Dragon color for quick identification

p: Sewn eyes are compact and consistent, so the cord sits neatly in a carabiner and the hitch dresses the same way every time. Tie your preferred hitch, add a micro pulley above it if you tend with one hand, and set it before every climb.
Courant makes ropes and hitch cords for tree work, and Phoenix is one of its hitch cord options. As with any cord, how it grips depends on the rope you pair it with.

Matching cord to rope is the part that takes time. A cord that grips perfectly on one line may slip or bind on another, especially when the rope is new and slick or old and fuzzy. Try a few wrap counts and hitch styles low to the ground, and note what works for each of your climbing lines.

Check the cord for glazing and stiffness and look closely at the sewn terminations for cut or abraded stitching. Retire it after a hard fall, heat damage, or any doubt. Do not try to repair sewn eyes yourself.

Compare other eye-and-eye prusiks. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Can I retie or shorten a sewn eye-to-eye prusik?
faq.a: No. Sewn terminations should not be altered. Buy the length you need.

faq.q: Will this cord work on my rope?
faq.a: 8 mm cord is often used on 11 to 13 mm climbing lines, but always test the hitch low on your rope first.

name: Multi-Purpose Ring Sling
title: Multi-Purpose Ring Sling for Climbing and Rigging
meta: A multi-purpose ring sling gives arborists a quick anchor, false crotch, or redirect. See common uses, how to choose one, and what to check before using it.
tagline: A versatile sling with a ring for anchors, redirects, and false crotches.
summary: A multi-purpose ring sling is a simple loop with a ring that wraps a stem or limb to make a quick anchor, redirect, or false crotch. It earns its spot in the gear bag on almost every job.
highlights: Wraps a limb or stem for a quick anchor
Ring gives a smooth bearing surface
Useful for redirects and false crotches
Packs small on the saddle or in the bag

p: Choke the sling around a sound limb and you have an instant redirect to keep your line out of a bad crotch, or a false crotch that protects the bark. The ring gives the rope a smooth surface and makes it easier to retrieve the sling from the ground in some setups.
Climbers also use one to set a temporary anchor while repositioning, or to hang a bag or saw out of the way.

Choose the sling length to suit the stems you usually work around. A short sling suits small limbs and keeps the ring close; a longer one wraps bigger wood and gives you room to choke it neatly. Many climbers carry two lengths so they are not forced to compromise on a tight union.

Only use a sling rated for the job you are giving it, and keep life-support uses separate from general rigging. Check the sling and ring for cuts, wear, and heat damage before every use, and never put a ring sling in a running rigging load it is not designed for.

See our other eye-and-eye cords and slings. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Can a ring sling be used as a false crotch?
faq.a: Yes, that is a common use. Choose one rated for life support and follow the manufacturer's instructions.

faq.q: Is a ring sling the same as a friction saver?
faq.a: Not quite. A friction saver usually has two rings or a ring and pulley built for an adjustable or retrievable setup. A ring sling is simpler.

name: Samson Bail Out XL Sewn Eye-to-Eye Hitch Cord
title: Samson Bail Out XL Sewn Eye-to-Eye Hitch Cord
h1: Samson Bail Out XL Sewn Eye-to-Eye Hitch Cord
meta: The Samson Bail Out XL is a sewn eye-to-eye hitch cord for friction hitches on climbing lines. Learn how to pair it with your rope and when to retire it.
tagline: A sewn eye-to-eye hitch cord from Samson for friction-hitch climbing.
summary: The Samson Bail Out XL is a sewn eye-to-eye hitch cord for climbers who tie a friction hitch on MRS or SRS. Samson's Bail Out cord is built to handle the heat a hitch sees, and the XL gives you a longer cord to work with.
highlights: Samson Bail Out hitch cord
Sewn eyes at both ends
XL length for more wraps or longer hitches
For Distel, VT, and similar hitches

p: A longer cord gives you room for extra wraps or a hitch that needs more tail, such as a VT on a slick rope. Climbers on bigger-diameter lines or heavier kits often reach for an XL cord so the hitch grips without having to be over-tightened.
Test it low on your climbing line, tend it with a micro pulley, and dress the hitch the same way every time so it behaves predictably.

Heavier climbers, or anyone carrying a big saw and a full rack, often find a hitch needs more grip than a standard-length cord gives. A longer cord lets you add wraps or braids to the hitch without running out of tail. Just keep the hitch neat and dressed, because extra length can also mean extra slack if it is set sloppily.
Look for glazing, stiff sections, and worn stitching at the eyes before each climb. Retire the cord after any heat damage or shock load, and never alter the sewn terminations.
Store spare hitch cords in a dry pouch away from sunlight and chemicals, and date them when they go into service so you know how long each one has been working.

Compare more eye-and-eye prusiks. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: What does XL mean on this hitch cord?
faq.a: It is a longer version of the cord. Check the listing for the exact length before you order.

faq.q: Which hitch should I tie with it?
faq.a: Distel and VT hitches are common choices. Use the hitch you were trained on and test it low first.

name: Sterling FLEX 8mm Sewn Eye-to-Eye Prusik
title: Sterling FLEX 8mm Sewn Eye-to-Eye Prusik
meta: The Sterling FLEX hitch cord is an 8 mm sewn eye-to-eye prusik for friction hitches. Learn how it handles, how to pair it with rope, and when to replace it.
tagline: Sterling's supple 8 mm hitch cord with sewn eyes for friction-hitch climbing.
summary: The Sterling FLEX hitch cord is an 8 mm sewn eye-to-eye prusik made for tying friction hitches on arborist climbing lines. As the name suggests, it is known for a supple hand that sets and releases easily.
highlights: 8 mm Sterling FLEX hitch cord
Supple feel that dresses easily
Sewn eyes at both ends
For Distel, VT, and other friction hitches

p: A softer hitch cord wraps tightly around the rope, so it can grab with fewer wraps and release with a light touch on the hitch. That makes FLEX popular with climbers who want smooth tending on long ascents and limb walks.
Every rope behaves differently, so tie your hitch and test it low before you go up. Add a micro pulley above the hitch to tend slack with one hand.

Soft cords can feel grabby on a fuzzy rope and slick on a brand-new one, so give your rope a few climbs to settle before you judge the pairing. If the hitch locks too hard, remove a wrap; if it slips, add one or try a different hitch. Small changes make a big difference in how the system tends.

Check the cord for glazed, stiff, or flattened sections and examine the sewn eyes for wear. Supple cords can show heat damage sooner on fast descents, so inspect after every climb and retire it at the first sign of trouble.
Keep a spare FLEX or similar cord in your bag. If your working cord glazes on a long descent mid-job, swapping it on the ground takes a minute and keeps you climbing safely.

See our other eye-and-eye prusiks. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: What is the difference between Sterling FLEX and RIT?
faq.a: Both are Sterling 8 mm hitch cords. FLEX is known for a softer, more supple hand, while RIT is generally chosen for durability. Check Sterling's listings for construction details.

faq.q: Does FLEX work on SRS?
faq.a: Many climbers use hitch cords on SRS rope wrench setups. Follow the device manufacturer's instructions and test low first.

name: Sterling RIT 8mm Sewn Eye-to-Eye Prusik
title: Sterling RIT 8mm Sewn Eye-to-Eye Prusik
meta: The Sterling RIT hitch cord is an 8 mm sewn eye-to-eye prusik built for durability on friction hitches. See how it handles and what to inspect each climb.
tagline: Sterling's durable 8 mm hitch cord with sewn eyes for friction hitches.
summary: The Sterling RIT hitch cord is an 8 mm sewn eye-to-eye prusik for climbers who want a hitch cord that stands up to heat and heavy use. It ties the usual friction hitches and suits busy production climbing.
highlights: 8 mm Sterling RIT hitch cord
Built for durability under heat and abrasion
Sewn eyes at both ends
For Distel, VT, and other friction hitches

p: Hitch cords take a beating on long descents and repeated tending. RIT is the cord climbers tend to choose when they want something that lasts, at the cost of a slightly firmer hand than softer cords. Expect a short break-in before it feels settled.
Pair it with your climbing line, test the hitch low, and tend it with a micro pulley for smooth slack management.

Climbers who descend fast, work big removals, or climb every day tend to wear through hitch cords quickly. A durable cord reduces how often you swap it out, which also means fewer changes to how your hitch behaves. That consistency is worth something when you are focused on the cut rather than the system.
Even a durable cord wears out. Look for glazing, stiffness, and worn stitching at the eyes before every climb, and retire the cord after any heat damage or shock load.
Record when each cord goes into service. Even durable hitch cord loses grip consistency as it wears, and a written date helps you spot when a cord has simply done its time.

Compare other eye-and-eye prusiks. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Is RIT stiffer than FLEX?
faq.a: RIT generally has a firmer feel than FLEX and is chosen for durability. Try both if you can and pick the one that suits your rope and hitch.

faq.q: What rope does an 8 mm cord suit?
faq.a: It is commonly used on 11 to 13 mm climbing lines. Always test the hitch on your actual rope.

name: Yale Veritas 8mm Sewn Eye-to-Eye Hitch Cord
title: Yale Veritas 8mm Sewn Eye-to-Eye Hitch Cord
h1: Yale Veritas 8mm Sewn Eye-to-Eye Hitch Cord
meta: The Yale Veritas hitch cord is an 8 mm sewn eye-to-eye cord for friction hitches on climbing lines. See how to pair it with rope and when to retire it.

summary: The Yale Veritas hitch cord is an 8 mm sewn eye-to-eye cord for tying friction hitches on arborist climbing lines. Yale is a familiar name in tree-care rope, and Veritas is its hitch cord option for MRS and SRS climbers.
highlights: 8 mm Yale Veritas hitch cord
Sewn eyes at both ends
For Distel, VT, and other friction hitches
Suits MRS and hitch-based SRS setups

Many climbers like running Yale hitch cord on Yale climbing lines, but any properly matched rope will do. The hitch is what matters.

If you are setting up a new system, write down which rope, which hitch, and how many wraps you settled on with the cord. When the cord wears out, replacing it with the same product and setup gets you back to the same behavior quickly, without a fresh round of trial and error at the base of the tree.
Check for glazing, stiff spots, and worn sewn eyes before every climb. Retire the cord after heat damage, a shock load, or anything that makes you doubt it.
Store hitch cords in a dry pouch, out of sunlight and away from fuel and bar oil, and keep them separate from rigging gear so they are never borrowed for a pull line or sling.

faq.q: Do I need Yale rope to use Veritas?
faq.a: No. It can be paired with other climbing lines. Test the hitch low on whatever rope you use.

faq.q: How many wraps should I use?
faq.a: That depends on your hitch, rope, and body weight. Follow your training and test low before climbing.

name: FS-FLEX 285 Pro Fall Protection Harness with Hip D-Rings
title: FS-FLEX 285 Pro Fall Protection Harness, Hip D-Rings
h1: FS-FLEX 285 Pro Fall Protection Harness with Hip D-Rings
meta: The FS-FLEX 285 Pro is a full-body fall protection harness with hip D-rings for aerial lift work. See how it fits and what to check before every shift.
tagline: A full-body fall protection harness with hip D-rings for bucket and lift work.
summary: The FS-FLEX 285 Pro is a full-body fall protection harness with hip D-rings, suited to aerial lift and bucket truck work. The dorsal connection handles fall arrest, while the hip D-rings give you positioning options.
highlights: Full-body fall protection harness
Hip D-rings for work positioning
Dorsal attachment for fall arrest
Suited to aerial lift and bucket truck work
Adjustable for fit

p: In an aerial lift, the harness connects to the boom's anchor with a lanyard sized to keep you in the bucket. The dorsal D-ring is the fall-arrest point. Hip D-rings are for work positioning, not for arresting a fall.
Adjust the leg and chest straps so the harness is snug with your normal work clothes on, and make sure the dorsal ring sits between the shoulder blades.

Arborists who work from a bucket truck still need a proper fall protection harness, even when they also climb with a tree saddle on other jobs. Keep the two systems separate and know which one the job calls for. Size the harness carefully, because a harness that is too loose can let you slip out or slide during a fall.

Check webbing, stitching, buckles, and every D-ring before each shift. Take any harness out of service after a fall or if you find cuts, burns, or chemical damage. Store it clean and dry, out of sunlight.

Write the harness's first-use date in your inspection log, and follow the manufacturer's guidance on service life. A competent person should inspect the harness at the interval your safety program requires.

See other fall arrest gear for aerial lifts. Fall protection must meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, be inspected before every shift, and be used only by workers trained on it.

faq.q: Can I use the hip D-rings for fall arrest?
faq.a: No. Hip D-rings are for work positioning. Connect fall arrest equipment to the dorsal D-ring per the manufacturer's instructions.

faq.q: Is a fall protection harness the same as a tree climbing saddle?
faq.a: No. A full-body harness is built for fall arrest in lifts. A tree saddle is a work-positioning harness for climbing.

name: Safewaze Arc Flash Nylon Full Body Harness
title: Safewaze Arc Flash Nylon Full Body Harness
h1: Safewaze Arc Flash Nylon Full Body Harness
meta: The Safewaze arc flash harness is a nylon full-body fall arrest harness for lift work near energized lines. Learn what to check and who it is for.
tagline: A nylon full-body fall arrest harness built for work near electrical hazards.
summary: The Safewaze arc flash harness is a nylon full-body fall arrest harness designed for crews working near energized lines, such as line-clearance tree work from a bucket. It is built with arc flash exposure in mind, unlike a general-purpose harness.
highlights: Full-body fall arrest harness
Designed for arc flash environments
Nylon webbing construction
Suits bucket truck and aerial lift work
specs: Aerial lift work near electrical hazards

p: Line-clearance crews face a hazard most tree workers do not: an electrical arc. Standard harness hardware and webbing are not designed for that exposure. An arc flash harness is built so the harness itself does not add to the hazard, and it pairs with the rest of your arc-rated PPE.
Only qualified line-clearance arborists should work near energized conductors, and the harness is one part of a full safety program.

Arc-rated gear only works as a system. Your clothing, gloves, face protection, and harness all need to suit the hazard level identified for the job. Talk to your safety lead about the arc rating your work requires, and check that the harness labeling matches before it goes in the bucket.

Adjust the harness so it is snug over your arc-rated clothing, with the dorsal attachment centered between the shoulder blades. Inspect webbing, stitching, and hardware before each shift, and remove it from service after any arc exposure or fall.
Keep the harness in a clean bag in the truck cab rather than loose in a bin. Contamination from oil or dirt can affect both webbing strength and arc performance.

See more aerial lift fall arrest gear. Fall protection must meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, be inspected before every shift, and be used only by workers trained on it.

faq.q: Does an arc flash harness make it safe to touch power lines?
faq.a: No. It is designed so the harness is not an added hazard during an arc event. Minimum approach distances and line-clearance rules still apply.

faq.q: Who should use this harness?
faq.a: Workers trained and qualified for line-clearance or utility work from aerial lifts.

name: Gap Arborist Supply Aerial Lift Evacuation Kit
title: Aerial Lift Evacuation Kit for Bucket Truck Crews
h1: Gap Arborist Supply Aerial Lift Evacuation Kit
meta: An aerial lift evacuation kit lets a trained bucket operator get down if the boom fails. See what the kit is for, how crews store it, and training to plan for.
tagline: A bagged emergency descent kit for bucket truck and aerial lift crews.
summary: An aerial lift evacuation kit is an emergency descent system that lets a trained worker get out of a stuck bucket when the boom will not bring them down. It lives in the bucket so it is there when needed.
highlights: Emergency descent kit for aerial lifts
Stored ready in the bucket
Meant for trained bucket operators
Bagged to keep components clean and together

p: Hydraulic failures, a stuck boom, or a medical problem can leave an operator in the bucket with no way down. An evacuation kit gives a trained worker a controlled descent from the bucket to the ground while the crew handles the emergency below.
Keep the kit in the bucket where it can be reached quickly, and make sure everyone who runs the lift knows where it is and how it is anchored.

Contents of evacuation kits vary, but most combine a length of rope, a descent control device, connectors, and a bag that keeps everything ready and clean. Learn exactly what is in your kit and how it connects to your harness and the boom anchor. Check it whenever the truck is serviced, not only when you remember.

Practice with the kit under supervision at a safe height before you ever need it. Check the bag, rope, and hardware on a regular schedule, keep it out of oil and hydraulic fluid, and replace any component that is damaged or has been used in a real descent.
See other fall protection gear. Fall protection must meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, be inspected before every shift, and be used only by workers trained on it.

faq.q: Who should use an aerial lift evacuation kit?
faq.a: Only workers trained in its use. Plan rescue and evacuation procedures with your crew before work starts.

faq.q: Does the kit replace a rescue plan?
faq.a: No. It is one tool within your emergency plan, which should also cover aerial rescue and first aid.

name: Husqvarna X-Guard Biodegradable Bar and Chain Oil (Gallon)
title: Husqvarna X-Guard Biodegradable Bar and Chain Oil
h1: Husqvarna X-Guard Biodegradable Bar and Chain Oil (Gallon)
meta: Husqvarna X-Guard is a biodegradable bar and chain oil in a gallon jug for chainsaw work. See where it makes sense, how to use it, and its typical price.
tagline: Husqvarna's biodegradable bar and chain oil for saws working near soil and water.
summary: Husqvarna X-Guard is a biodegradable bar and chain oil sold by the gallon for crews who want to cut down the oil they leave in yards, soil, and waterways. It keeps the bar and chain lubricated like any bar oil while breaking down more readily.
highlights: Biodegradable bar and chain oil
One-gallon jug
For chainsaws and pole saws with auto oilers
Good choice near gardens, lawns, and water

p: Every saw throws oil off the chain while it cuts, and on a tree job that oil lands in lawns, flower beds, and sometimes creeks. A biodegradable oil reduces that footprint, which matters to many residential and municipal customers.
Fill the oil tank every time you fill the fuel tank, and check that the bar is wet before you start cutting. A dry chain stretches and dulls quickly and wears the bar.

A gallon jug is the practical size for most crews: enough for several days of saw work, small enough to carry to the fuel station on the truck. Pour carefully, wipe up spills, and keep the cap clean so sawdust and grit do not end up in your saw's oil tank and pump.
Keep the jug sealed and out of extreme heat or cold. Some biodegradable oils can gum up if a saw sits for a long time, so run the saw or follow Husqvarna's storage advice before long breaks.
Store the jug off the floor of the truck so it does not crack or tip, and keep it away from your climbing and rigging bags so a leak never reaches soft goods.
See more saw fluids. Never mix bar oil into fuel, and wear proper PPE when running a saw.

faq.q: Can I use X-Guard in any brand of chainsaw?
faq.a: Bar and chain oil is generally compatible across brands. Check your saw's manual for any oil requirements.

faq.q: Is biodegradable oil as good as regular bar oil?
faq.a: It is designed to lubricate the bar and chain in normal use. Watch for adequate oil flow and follow storage guidance for long breaks.

name: CAMP Turbospur Ascender System
title: CAMP Turbospur Foot Ascender System for SRS
meta: The CAMP Turbospur is a foot ascender system for climbing a single rope. See how foot ascenders speed up SRS ascents and what to check before using one.
tagline: A foot ascender system from CAMP for faster rope ascents on SRS.
summary: The CAMP Turbospur ascender system is a foot ascender setup from CAMP for climbers who want to walk up a single rope rather than haul themselves up it. It works alongside your main SRS ascent system to save energy on long ascents.
highlights: Foot ascender system from CAMP
Lets you step up the rope on SRS
Works with your main ascent system
Saves energy on tall climbs

p: On a single rope, a foot ascender grabs the line below your main ascent system so you can stand up and push with your legs instead of pulling with your arms. Paired with a chest or handled ascender above, it turns a tiring ascent into a steady rope walk.
It is a big help on tall trees and repeated climbs in a day.

If you are new to SRS, get comfortable with your main ascent system first, then add a foot ascender once the basics are second nature. Practice switching from ascent to work mode and back, and make sure the foot ascender never interferes with your changeover to descent.

Fit the foot attachment to your boot with no loose straps, and learn to release the ascender cleanly before you climb high. Inspect the cam, teeth, and frame for wear and keep the device clean of sap and grit.
Store the foot ascender with your climbing kit, clean and dry, and check the cam spring action before every climb. A weak spring can cause the cam to slip or release when you least expect it.

See other foot ascenders and foot loops. A foot ascender is never your only point of attachment. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Is a foot ascender part of my life-support system?
faq.a: No. It assists the ascent. Your main ascent system and saddle attachment carry your life support.

faq.q: Will it work on my rope?
faq.a: Check CAMP's instructions for the rope diameter range the device is designed for.

name: ISC Stryder Foot Ascender
title: ISC Stryder Foot Ascender for Rope Walking
meta: The ISC Stryder is a foot ascender for SRS climbers who want to walk up the rope instead of pulling. See how it fits into your ascent kit and what to inspect.
tagline: A foot ascender from ISC for walking up a single rope.
summary: The ISC Stryder foot ascender clips the rope at your boot so you can push with your legs on an SRS ascent. ISC makes a wide range of arborist hardware, and the Stryder is its option for climbers who want a more efficient climb.
highlights: Foot ascender from ISC
Mounts at the boot for leg-powered ascents
Pairs with a chest or handled ascender
Reduces arm fatigue on tall climbs

p: A foot ascender holds the rope below your other ascent gear. Step up, stand, slide your upper device, and repeat. The motion feels like climbing stairs and uses your strongest muscles, which keeps you fresher for the work at the top.
Most climbers put it on the right foot and practice releasing it smoothly before moving to a working height.

Fit matters more than you would expect. A foot ascender that twists on your boot or catches the rope at a poor angle will slow you down. Spend time on the ground adjusting the strap and practicing the stride, and keep your rope weighted at the bottom if it tends to lift as you step.
Check the cam, spring, and teeth for wear and debris, and inspect the foot strap or attachment before each climb. Keep it clean of sap and grit so it grips and releases cleanly.
Store the ascender clean and dry with your climbing kit, and keep the cam free of sap and grit. A cam that sticks or springs back slowly needs cleaning or replacing before your next climb.

Compare other foot ascenders and foot loops. A foot ascender is not a life-support connection. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Which foot does a foot ascender go on?
faq.a: Most climbers use the right foot, but use whichever feels natural and matches your training.

faq.q: Can I descend with a foot ascender attached?
faq.a: You need to release it from the rope before changing over to descent. Follow the manufacturer's instructions.

name: Ocean Polyester Footlock Prusik
title: Ocean Polyester Footlock Prusik Loop
meta: The Ocean polyester footlock prusik is a hitch loop for footlocking a doubled rope. See how footlock prusiks work, how to fit one, and what to check first.
tagline: A polyester prusik loop for footlocking up a doubled climbing line.
summary: The Ocean polyester footlock prusik is a hitch loop that ties around a doubled rope so you can footlock up it and rest on the hitch between steps. Polyester construction gives a firm, durable cord for this job.
highlights: Polyester footlock prusik loop
For footlocking a doubled rope
Holds you between footlock strokes
Classic climbing technique gear

p: Footlocking is a classic way to ascend a doubled rope: you lock the rope between your feet, stand, and slide a prusik up above you. The prusik loop clips to your saddle and holds you when you sit back. It is fast once learned and needs very little gear.
The loop must be the right length for your height so it stays in reach above your head as you climb.

Footlocking is still taught and used, especially for getting into a tree with a high, clean tie-in point. It is fast and uses little gear, but it is tiring if your technique is off. Learn it with a trainer, keep your stroke short and steady, and rest on the prusik whenever you need to.
Test the prusik on your rope low to the ground. Inspect the cord for glazing, cuts, and stiff sections, and retire it after any heat damage. Footlocking takes practice, so learn it under supervision.
Keep footlock prusiks separate from your working hitch cords so you always grab the right loop. Mark the length on a tag or with tape if you carry more than one size.

See more hitch cord and split tails. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: What length footlock prusik do I need?
faq.a: It depends on your height and how you climb. It should keep the hitch within easy reach above your head.

faq.q: Can I footlock a single rope?
faq.a: Footlocking is normally done on a doubled line with a prusik that grabs both legs of the rope. Follow your training.

name: Arborist Crane Tie-In Point with Yale Rope
title: Arborist Crane Tie-In Point with Yale Rope
h1: Arborist Crane Tie-In Point with Yale Rope
meta: An arborist crane tie-in point gives climbers a dedicated attachment on the crane line during crane-assisted removals. See how it is used and who it suits.
tagline: A dedicated climber tie-in for crane-assisted tree removals.
summary: An arborist crane tie-in point gives a climber a dedicated, separate attachment on the crane line during crane-assisted removals. This version is built with Yale rope and is meant for crews who regularly work under a crane.
highlights: Dedicated climber tie-in for crane work
Built with Yale rope
Keeps climber attachment separate from the load
For crane-assisted removals

p: On crane jobs, a climber may need to ride or tie in to the crane line to reach the pick point. A dedicated tie-in point keeps the climber's connection separate from the rigging that holds the load, which is a core principle of crane-assisted tree work.

How and when a climber may be attached to a crane is governed by ANSI Z133, crane regulations, and the crane operator's procedures. Plan the job with the operator and qualified signal person before anyone ties in.

Crane-assisted removals can make dangerous trees much safer to take down, but only when the crane crew and tree crew share a clear plan. Agree on signals, load weights, cut sequence, and where the climber will be at every pick. Keep the tie-in point stored with your life-support gear and check it before every crane job.

Inspect the rope, terminations, and any hardware before every use. Retire it after a shock load or any damage. Never use it as a rigging sling, and keep it with your life-support gear, not the rigging kit.

See other friction savers and tie-in points. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Can any climber tie in to a crane?
faq.a: No. Crane-assisted tree work requires trained, qualified workers and must follow ANSI Z133, crane regulations, and the operator's procedures.

faq.q: Can this be used to rig a pick?
faq.a: No. It is a climber attachment only. Keep life-support gear separate from rigging.

name: CAMP Herbol Cambium Saver
title: CAMP Herbol Cambium Saver for Tree Climbing
meta: The CAMP Herbol cambium saver protects bark and your rope at the tie-in point. See how a cambium saver works on MRS and SRS and what to inspect before climbing.
tagline: A cambium saver from CAMP that protects the tree and your climbing line.
summary: The CAMP Herbol cambium saver goes over a limb at your tie-in point so your climbing line runs on hardware instead of bark. It reduces friction, protects the cambium, and saves wear on your rope.
highlights: Cambium saver from CAMP
Protects bark at the tie-in point
Reduces rope friction and wear
For MRS climbing and SRS anchors

p: Running a climbing line straight over a limb wears through bark, heats the rope, and adds friction to every move. A cambium saver separates the rope from the tree, so you climb smoother and leave less damage behind, which matters on pruning jobs where the tree stays.
Install it from the ground with a throw line or set it as you climb, depending on your system.

A cambium saver also makes your climb smoother. With the rope running on hardware instead of bark, your hitch advances more easily and you lose less energy on every move. On repeat jobs in the same tree, it protects the tie-in union from the damage that builds up when rope saws back and forth over time.
Check the rings or hardware and the connecting sling or rope for wear, grooves, and cuts. Make sure the saver sits on a sound limb that is sized for the load.
Store the saver with your climbing kit, clean and dry, and keep it away from rigging gear. A saver that has been used for rigging loads should not go back into life-support service.
See other friction savers. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Is a cambium saver the same as a friction saver?
faq.a: Yes, the terms are used for the same kind of device.

faq.q: Can I use it for SRS?
faq.a: Some climbers use a friction saver as a canopy anchor on SRS. Follow CAMP's instructions for approved uses.

name: CMI Friction Saver with Aluminum Rings
title: CMI Friction Saver with Aluminum Rings
h1: CMI Friction Saver with Aluminum Rings
meta: The CMI friction saver with aluminum rings protects bark and rope at your tie-in. See how ring-and-ring savers work, how to retrieve them, and what to check.
tagline: A ring-and-ring friction saver from CMI with light aluminum rings.
summary: The CMI friction saver with aluminum rings is a classic ring-and-ring design that keeps your climbing line off the bark at the tie-in point. Aluminum rings keep it light on the saddle and in the throw-line setup.
highlights: Ring-and-ring friction saver
Aluminum rings for light weight
Protects bark and reduces rope wear
Retrievable from the ground

p: One ring is larger than the other. Set the saver over a limb with a throw line, pass your climbing line through both rings, and the rope runs smoothly on metal instead of bark. When you finish, a retrieval line lets the small ring pass through the large one so the saver comes down to the ground.
It is a simple, proven setup for MRS climbing, especially on pruning work.

Ring-and-ring savers are popular because they are simple and easy to retrieve. Set it on a sound union high in the tree with a throw line, then install your climbing line from the ground. When the job is finished, retrieve it carefully so the rings do not hit anyone working below.

Aluminum wears faster than steel, so check the rings for grooves and sharp edges before every climb. Inspect the connecting strap or rope too. Retire the saver if the rings show deep wear or the strap is damaged.

Keep the retrieval line separate and clearly marked so it is never mistaken for your climbing line. Check that the saver has fully cleared the union before you pull it down, and call out before it falls.
Compare more friction savers. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Aluminum or steel rings?
faq.a: Aluminum is lighter. Steel lasts longer under heavy rope wear. Choose based on how often you climb and how much weight you carry.

faq.q: How do I retrieve a ring-and-ring friction saver?
faq.a: Use the retrieval method in the manufacturer's instructions, typically by pulling the small ring through the large ring.

name: Gap Arborist Supply OP Friction Saver
title: OP Friction Saver for Arborist Climbing
h1: Gap Arborist Supply OP Friction Saver
meta: The OP friction saver keeps your climbing line off the bark at the tie-in point and cuts rope wear. Learn how friction savers work and what to check before use.
tagline: A straightforward friction saver for protecting bark and rope at the tie-in.
summary: The OP friction saver is a simple friction saver that sits over your tie-in limb so the climbing line runs on hardware instead of bark. It is a practical everyday piece of kit for MRS climbing and pruning work.
highlights: Simple friction saver for everyday climbing
Protects bark at the tie-in point
Reduces heat and wear on your climbing line
Sets with a throw line from the ground

p: A friction saver separates your rope from the tree at the tie-in. That means less friction when you advance your hitch, less heat in the rope, and less damage to the cambium, which is a priority on trees that stay standing after the job.
Set it with a throw line over a sound union, run your climbing line through it, and check that it sits cleanly before you weight it.

Friction savers come in a few styles, including ring-and-ring, ring and pulley, and adjustable designs. A simple saver like this suits everyday climbing on straightforward tie-in points. If you climb on SRS, check the manufacturer's instructions before using any friction saver as an anchor.
Look over the hardware for grooves or sharp edges and the strap or rope for cuts and wear before every climb. Retire it if anything looks doubtful.
Store the saver with your climbing kit and never use it in a rigging setup. Rigging loads can groove hardware and damage the strap in ways that make it unsafe for climbing.

See our full range of friction savers. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Do I need a friction saver for every climb?
faq.a: It is good practice on most climbs, especially when the tree is being pruned and kept. It protects the tree and your rope.

faq.q: What limb should I set it on?
faq.a: A live, sound limb or union sized for your load. Assess the tie-in carefully before you climb.

name: Safewaze Comfort Leg Pads
title: Safewaze Comfort Leg Pads for Full-Body Harnesses
meta: Safewaze comfort leg pads add cushioning to harness leg straps for long shifts in a lift or on a structure. See how they fit and what to check on inspection.
tagline: Add-on padding for harness leg straps on long days.
summary: Safewaze comfort leg pads are add-on harness leg pads that cushion the leg straps of a full-body harness, which helps on long shifts in an aerial lift. They spread the pressure of the straps so the harness is easier to wear all day.
highlights: Add-on padding for harness leg straps
Spreads strap pressure for comfort
Helps on long aerial lift shifts
From Safewaze

body.h: Comfort that keeps you wearing it
p: A harness that rubs gets loosened or left in the truck. Padding the leg straps makes a full-body harness easier to wear correctly for a full shift, which is the point of fall protection.
Fit the pads so they do not change how the straps sit or how the buckles close.

Workers in bucket trucks often stand in the same spot for hours, and leg straps can press on the same area all day. Pads help reduce that pressure. They are a small add-on that can make a big difference to whether a crew member keeps the harness adjusted properly from morning to quitting time.
Use pads that are approved for your harness, and follow Safewaze's instructions. When you inspect the harness, slide the pads aside so you can see the webbing and stitching underneath.
Keep the pads clean and dry along with the harness. If the pads become torn or contaminated with oil or chemicals, replace them, and inspect the harness underneath for the same damage.
See more fall protection gear. Fall protection must meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, be inspected before every shift, and be used only by workers trained on it.

faq.q: Will leg pads fit any harness?
faq.a: Check the manufacturer's compatibility information. Pads should not alter how the harness fits or functions.

faq.q: Do I still inspect under the pads?
faq.a: Yes. Move the pads aside and inspect the webbing and stitching beneath them.

name: CAMP Spacecraft 45 L Gear Bag
title: CAMP Spacecraft 45 L Gear Bag for Climbing Kit
meta: The CAMP Spacecraft 45 L is a gear bag sized to carry a climbing kit to the job. See what fits, how arborists pack it, and why a dedicated bag protects gear.
tagline: A 45-liter gear bag from CAMP for hauling climbing kit to the job.
summary: The CAMP Spacecraft 45 L gear bag is a 45-liter pack for arborists who want their climbing kit together in one place. It has room for a saddle, hardware, and smaller lines, and keeps them out of the sawdust and oil in the truck.
highlights: 45-liter gear bag from CAMP
Room for a saddle and hardware
Keeps climbing gear away from fuel and oil
Carries to the tree as one load

body.h: What fits in a 45 L bag
p: A 45-liter bag holds a saddle, a rack of carabiners and devices, hitch cords, a lanyard, and throw line, with room left over for a helmet in many setups. Your main climbing line usually goes in its own rope bag.
Packing the same way every time makes it obvious when something is missing before you leave the shop.

Keep a small checklist in the bag so you can confirm before leaving the shop that your saddle, hitch cords, lanyard, throw line, and carabiners are all there. A forgotten piece of life-support gear can end a climbing day before it starts.

Bar oil, fuel, and battery acid can damage soft goods without visible signs. A dedicated bag keeps the kit clean and separate from saws and fluids. Empty and dry it after wet days so gear does not sit damp.
Store the bag somewhere dry and away from fuel and bar oil. If something leaks onto it, check every piece of soft gear inside before it goes back into service, and retire anything contaminated.
See more gear bags. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Will a 45 L bag hold my climbing rope?
faq.a: Some shorter lines may fit, but most climbers keep the main rope in a separate rope bag.

faq.q: Why not just keep gear in a truck box?
faq.a: Shared boxes expose soft goods to fuel, oil, and sharp tools. A dedicated bag protects life-support gear.

name: DMM Porter 45 Liter Gear Bag
title: DMM Porter 45 Liter Gear Bag for Arborists
meta: The DMM Porter is a 45 liter gear bag for carrying climbing and rigging kit. See what it holds, how arborists use it on the job, and how to keep gear clean.
tagline: DMM's 45-liter gear bag for moving climbing and rigging kit.
summary: The DMM Porter gear bag is a 45 liter haul bag for arborists who want one tough bag for saddle, hardware, and smaller lines. It is built to be dragged around job sites and still keep gear organized.
highlights: 45-liter gear bag from DMM
Holds saddle, hardware, and small lines
Tough build for job-site handling
Keeps kit separated from saws and fluids

p: Carry the Porter to the base of the tree and stage your kit on a tarp or rope bag beside it. Having hardware, hitch cords, and lanyards in one place speeds up setup and makes it easy to check that everything comes back at the end of the day.
It also works as a rigging hardware bag for blocks, slings, and carabiners, if you keep rigging and climbing kit clearly separated.

A gear bag also makes it easier to keep track of when each item was inspected. Many crews tag or log their life-support gear, and having it all in one bag makes the daily check quick. If something looks damaged, set it aside and mark it so it is not used by mistake.
Shake out sawdust, keep the bag away from fuel cans and bar oil, and let it dry open after wet days. Inspect the gear you pull out of it before every climb.
Store the bag clean and dry, and never let it sit on the truck bed next to fuel cans or bar oil jugs. A small leak can contaminate everything inside without obvious signs.
Compare other gear bags. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Can I use one bag for climbing and rigging gear?
faq.a: It is better to keep them separate so life-support gear is never used for rigging.

faq.q: Is 45 liters big enough?
faq.a: For a saddle, hardware, and accessories, yes. Most climbers carry the main rope in a separate rope bag.

name: Notch Pro Access Bag
title: Notch Pro Access Bag for Climbing Gear
meta: The Notch Pro Access bag carries climbing gear with easy access on the job. See how arborists use it, what it suits, and how to keep life-support gear clean.
tagline: A Notch gear bag for keeping climbing kit organized and easy to reach.
summary: The Notch Pro Access bag is a gear bag for arborists who want their climbing kit organized and quick to get at on the job. Notch makes a wide range of tree climbing gear and accessories, and this bag is built for daily use.
highlights: Gear bag from Notch
Designed for quick access to kit
Keeps climbing gear separate and clean
Built for daily job-site use

p: On a busy job, digging for a carabiner or hitch cord wastes time. A bag that opens wide makes it easy to see your kit, check it, and get climbing. It also makes the end-of-day check simple: everything goes back where it came from.
Use it for climbing gear, or as a dedicated bag for rigging hardware if you keep the two kits apart.

For crews that share kit, a dedicated bag per climber helps prevent gear from getting mixed up. Each climber knows their own saddle, hitch cords, and hardware, and knows the history of each piece. That makes inspection and retirement decisions much easier.
Keep the bag away from fuel and bar oil, shake out sawdust, and dry it open after wet days. Check your gear as you pack and unpack it.
Clean the bag out regularly. Sawdust, sap, and grit work into hardware and soft goods, and a quick shake-out at the end of the week keeps your kit easier to inspect.
See other gear bags. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: What fits in the Notch Pro Access bag?
faq.a: Check the listing for capacity. Gear bags like this are generally sized for a saddle, hardware, and small lines.

faq.q: Should my climbing rope go in the same bag?
faq.a: Most climbers keep the main line in a separate rope bag to protect it.

name: Petzl Transport 45L Gear Pack
title: Petzl Transport 45L Gear Pack for Rope Work
meta: The Petzl Transport 45L is a rugged gear pack for hauling climbing and rope access kit. See what it holds, why arborists use it, and how to care for it.
tagline: Petzl's 45-liter haul pack for climbing and rope work gear.
summary: The Petzl Transport 45L is a rugged gear pack built for carrying climbing and rope work equipment to the job. Arborists use it to keep a saddle, hardware, and lines together and protected between the truck and the tree.
highlights: 45-liter gear pack from Petzl
Tough fabric for job-site use
Backpack carry to remote trees
Keeps kit separated from saws and fluids

p: When the tree is at the back of a property or down a slope, a pack with shoulder straps beats arm-carrying a bag. The Transport is a haul-style pack meant to take abuse, so it suits climbers who move their kit a long way on foot.
Pack heavy hardware low and close to your back, and keep the saddle on top for quick setup at the tree.

Carrying a pack instead of a bag also keeps your hands free for a saw, throw line, or rope bag. On long walks to a job, that alone can save a trip back to the truck. Adjust the shoulder straps before loading so the pack sits steady and does not swing as you walk.
Rinse off mud and sap, dry it open, and keep it away from fuel and bar oil in the truck. Inspect the gear you take out of it before every climb.
Store the pack open and dry when you get back to the shop. Damp gear that sits zipped up can develop mildew, and fabric soft goods may need to be retired if they stay wet too long.
See other gear bags. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Can the Transport 45L carry a climbing rope?
faq.a: Some ropes will fit along with other kit, depending on length. Many climbers still use a separate rope bag.

faq.q: Is it waterproof?
faq.a: Check Petzl's product information for the fabric and closure details. Dry your gear after wet days either way.

name: Fanno 15-Inch Curved Blade Hand Saw
title: Fanno 15-Inch Curved Blade Hand Saw for Pruning
meta: The Fanno 15-inch curved blade hand saw cuts fast on the pull stroke for pruning and climbing work. See where it fits on the saddle and how to look after it.
tagline: A 15-inch curved pull-stroke pruning saw for climbers and ground crews.
summary: The Fanno 15-inch curved blade hand saw is a pull-stroke pruning saw for climbers and ground workers who need clean cuts on limbs too big for loppers. The curve helps the teeth bite on overhead and awkward cuts.
highlights: 15-inch curved pruning blade
Cuts on the pull stroke
Good reach for overhead cuts
Suited to a scabbard on the saddle

body.h: Where a 15 inch curved saw shines
p: A 15-inch blade handles small to mid-size limbs in pruning cuts and deadwood work, and it is long enough to reach past a branch collar without crowding your hand. The curve pulls the teeth into the wood, which helps when you are cutting above your head or at an odd angle from the saddle.
Make a proper pruning cut just outside the branch collar, and undercut larger limbs to stop the bark from tearing.

Climbers often carry a curved saw on the saddle for fast limb removal and a smaller straight saw for detail cuts. A 15-inch blade sits in the middle, long enough for bigger cuts while still easy to handle on a lanyard. Keep your cuts controlled and clear of your rope and lanyard at all times.
Keep it in a scabbard on the saddle so the teeth are covered when not in use. Clean off sap after work, keep the blade dry, and replace the blade when it dulls rather than forcing it.
Keep a spare blade in the truck. On a big pruning job, switching to a sharp blade halfway through the day speeds up cutting and leaves cleaner wounds on the tree.
See other hand saws and scabbards. Always cut away from your lifeline and lanyard.

faq.q: Is a curved or straight blade better?
faq.a: Curved blades bite well on overhead and pulling cuts. Straight blades are often preferred for precise flush work. Many climbers carry one of each.

faq.q: Can I sharpen the blade?
faq.a: Most pull-stroke pruning saw teeth are hardened and are replaced rather than sharpened. Check the manufacturer's guidance.

name: 3M Peltor Over-the-Head Earmuffs
title: 3M Peltor Over-the-Head Earmuffs for Saw Work
meta: 3M Peltor over-the-head earmuffs protect your hearing around chainsaws and chippers. See when to wear them, how to get a good seal, and how they compare.
tagline: Over-the-head hearing protection from 3M Peltor for ground crews.
summary: 3M Peltor over-the-head earmuffs are simple hearing protectors for ground crews running saws, chippers, and stump grinders. They are quick to put on and take off between tasks.
highlights: Over-the-head hearing protection
From the 3M Peltor line
Quick on and off between tasks
For saw, chipper, and grinder noise

body.h: Protecting your hearing on the job
p: Chainsaws, chippers, and stump grinders are loud enough to cause permanent hearing loss over time. Earmuffs are the simplest fix: they go on in a second and come off when you need to talk to the crew.
Over-the-head muffs suit ground workers who are not wearing a helmet. If you wear a helmet all day, a helmet-mounted muff is usually a better fit.

Wear hearing protection whenever you are near running saws, chippers, or grinders, not just when you are running them yourself. Ground workers feeding a chipper or bucking near a felling cut get almost the same noise exposure as the operator. Keep spare muffs on the truck so nobody goes without.
Push hair away from the cushions, keep glasses temples thin, and check the cushions for cracks. Replace cushions and foam inserts when they harden or flatten, since a poor seal lets noise in.
Hearing loss from noise is gradual and permanent, so the habit matters more than any single day. Make muffs part of the kit you put on before starting any power equipment.
See other hearing protection. Check the noise reduction rating on the product label and match it to your exposure.

faq.q: Can I wear these with a helmet?
faq.a: Over-the-head muffs usually do not fit well under a helmet. Choose a helmet-mounted model for that.

faq.q: What noise reduction rating do I need?
faq.a: It depends on your exposure. Check the NRR on the product label and your employer's hearing conservation program.

name: Husqvarna Professional Helmet Hearing Muffs
title: Husqvarna Professional Helmet Hearing Muffs
meta: Husqvarna professional helmet hearing muffs clip to a compatible helmet to protect your hearing during saw work. See how they fit and when to replace parts.
tagline: Helmet-mounted hearing protection from Husqvarna for saw operators.
summary: Husqvarna professional helmet hearing muffs mount on a compatible helmet so your hearing protection goes wherever your hard hat does. They flip out of the way when you need to talk and lock back in place when the saw starts.
highlights: Helmet-mounted hearing protection
Flip up between cuts to talk to the crew
Designed for Husqvarna professional helmets
For chainsaw and chipper noise

p: When you wear a helmet all day, helmet-mounted muffs are the easiest way to keep hearing protection in place. There is no headband to fight with, and the muffs flip up when you need to listen for a call from the ground.
They suit fellers, climbers, and ground crews who run saws and chippers through the day.

Helmet-mounted muffs also stay with your helmet when it goes back in the truck, so they are less likely to be forgotten or lost than separate muffs. Check the mounting arms for cracks and loose fittings when you inspect your helmet, and replace any part that does not hold the muffs firmly in place.
Confirm the muffs are compatible with your helmet before ordering. Check that the cushions seal fully around your ears, and replace cushions and inserts when they harden or crack.
If you share helmets on a crew, assign each person their own muff cushions where possible. It is more hygienic and keeps each set fitted to the person wearing it.
Browse more hearing protection. Check the noise reduction rating on the label against your exposure.

faq.q: Will these fit any helmet?
faq.a: They are made for compatible Husqvarna helmets. Check the mounting system before ordering for a different helmet.

faq.q: Can I replace the ear cushions?
faq.a: Yes, cushions and inserts are wear items. Replace them when they harden, crack, or no longer seal.
